questions.stem: What is happening in Thebes when the play begins?
options: A civil war has broken out between Oedipus and Creon
A plague is killing the city's people, crops and herds
Laius has just been murdered, and the city is in mourning
The Sphinx is attacking travellers on the roads to the city
questions.explanation: A priest leads a crowd of suppliants to beg King Oedipus for help. Oedipus, who once saved Thebes from the Sphinx, promises to save it again.

questions.stem: What message does Creon bring back from Apollo's oracle at Delphi?
options: The plague will end when the killer of King Laius is found and driven out
The plague will end when Oedipus gives up the throne and leaves the city
The plague will end when the Thebans build a new temple to Apollo
The plague will end when Tiresias is put to death for his false prophecies
questions.explanation: Laius, the king before Oedipus, was killed years earlier and his murderer never found. Oedipus vows to hunt the killer down, not knowing he is hunting himself.

questions.stem: Oedipus curses Laius's unknown murderer, and even himself if the killer turns out to share his house. Why is this so powerful for the audience?
options: The audience knows the shepherd is the murderer, so Oedipus is cursing a witness
The audience knows Jocasta is the murderer, so Oedipus is cursing his wife
The audience knows Oedipus is the murderer, so he is cursing himself
The audience knows Creon is the murderer, so Oedipus is cursing his friend
questions.explanation: Sophocles' audience knew the myth. Every promise Oedipus makes to find the killer is dramatic irony, because each one will fall on his own head.

questions.stem: How does Tiresias respond when Oedipus asks him to name the killer?
options: He names the shepherd who survived the attack on Laius
He refuses at first, and when provoked he says Oedipus is the murderer
He names Creon as the killer and asks Oedipus to banish him at once
He says the killer died long ago, so the plague must have another cause
questions.explanation: Tiresias knows the truth and wishes he did not. Oedipus insults him until he speaks, then refuses to believe what he hears.

questions.stem: How does Oedipus explain Tiresias's accusation?
options: He believes Tiresias is simply too old and confused to read the signs properly
He believes Jocasta has asked Tiresias to frighten him into leaving Thebes
He believes Tiresias wants to seize the throne for himself
He believes Creon has bribed Tiresias as part of a plot to seize the throne
questions.explanation: Oedipus turns on Creon, his brother-in-law, and threatens him with death. His quick suspicion and anger show how fiercely he guards his power.

questions.stem: How does Creon defend himself against the charge of plotting?
options: He argues that he already has influence without the burdens of ruling
He admits that he wants the throne but denies that he ever bribed the prophet
He accuses Jocasta of turning Oedipus against her own brother
He offers to leave Thebes for ever if Oedipus will spare his life
questions.explanation: Creon says a sensible man would not swap a comfortable life of influence for the fears of a king. His calm reasoning contrasts with Oedipus's anger, and Jocasta and the Chorus urge Oedipus to let him go.

questions.stem: Why does Jocasta tell Oedipus the story of Laius's death?
options: To prove that Tiresias is honest, since he warned Laius about the robbers
To prove that prophecies cannot be trusted, since Laius's never came true
To prove that Creon could not have killed Laius, since he was in Corinth
To prove that Oedipus is not from Thebes, since he arrived after Laius died
questions.explanation: Laius was told he would die at the hands of his son, so the baby was abandoned on a mountain. Laius, she says, was killed by robbers where three roads meet, so the prophecy failed.

questions.stem: Which detail in Jocasta's story disturbs Oedipus?
options: That Laius was killed by a single man with a sword
That Laius was killed at a place where three roads meet
That Laius was travelling to Corinth to visit King Polybus
That Laius had a son who was raised by a shepherd
questions.explanation: Oedipus remembers killing an old man and his attendants at just such a crossroads. Jocasta's attempt to reassure him begins his unravelling.

questions.stem: Why did Oedipus leave Corinth as a young man?
options: He was sent to Thebes to defeat the Sphinx for a rich reward
He fell in love with Jocasta and wanted to marry her
An oracle said he would kill his father and marry his mother
He was banished by Polybus for insulting the god Apollo
questions.explanation: Believing Polybus and Merope were his parents, Oedipus fled Corinth to escape the prophecy. In running from his fate he ran straight towards it.

questions.stem: What news does the messenger from Corinth bring at first?
options: Polybus has died, and Corinth wants Oedipus to be its king
Merope has died, and Polybus wants Oedipus to come home
Corinth is at war with Thebes and demands Oedipus's surrender
Laius's killer has been caught on the road near Corinth
questions.explanation: Oedipus is relieved that the man he thinks is his father died of old age. For a moment the prophecy seems false, until the messenger tries to calm his fear about Merope.

questions.stem: What does the messenger then reveal about Oedipus's birth?
options: Oedipus was born in Corinth, but his mother was a servant in the palace of Polybus
Oedipus was found in a temple at Delphi and raised by the priests of Apollo
Polybus and Merope were not his parents; the messenger was given the baby by a shepherd
Polybus was his father but Merope was not his mother, so he is safe from the prophecy
questions.explanation: The messenger received the baby, with its ankles pinned, from one of Laius's shepherds on Mount Cithaeron, and gave him to the childless king and queen. Meant to help, the news brings disaster.

questions.stem: How does Jocasta react when she understands the messenger's story?
options: She accuses the messenger of lying and orders him to leave the city
She sends for Creon to take the throne before the shepherd arrives
She begs Oedipus to stop searching, then rushes into the palace
She tells the Chorus the whole truth and asks them to protect Oedipus
questions.explanation: Jocasta realises first. Oedipus thinks she fears he is of low birth, and declares he will find out who he is whatever it costs.

questions.stem: Why is the old shepherd so unwilling to answer Oedipus's questions?
options: He cannot remember anything about the baby he took to the mountain
He expects the Corinthian to share in a reward for the news
He knows the truth will destroy Oedipus and is forced to speak by threats
He believes the baby he took to Mount Cithaeron died there, as he was ordered
questions.explanation: The shepherd is also the only survivor of the attack on Laius, so he knows both halves of the truth. Under threat of torture he admits the baby came from Laius's house and that he gave it away out of pity.

questions.stem: What happens to Jocasta and Oedipus after the truth is revealed?
options: Jocasta takes her own life, and Oedipus blinds himself
Jocasta flees to Corinth, and Oedipus is put to death
Jocasta is banished by Creon, and Oedipus becomes a priest
Jocasta is imprisoned by Creon, and Oedipus flees to Corinth
questions.explanation: A messenger from the palace reports these events, which take place offstage. Oedipus then appears, blinded, to face the Chorus.

questions.stem: How does the play end?
options: Oedipus begs to be exiled, and Creon says he must first consult the gods
Oedipus is exiled at once by Creon, who then takes the throne
Oedipus kills himself after learning that Jocasta is dead
Oedipus hands his crown to Tiresias and asks the prophet to rule the city in his place
questions.explanation: Creon, now in charge, treats Oedipus fairly but carefully. Oedipus says goodbye to his young daughters, and the Chorus warns against calling anyone happy before death.

questions.stem: Which quality of Oedipus both makes him a great king and leads to his downfall?
options: His caution, which makes him wait for others before acting
His loyalty to Creon, which blinds him to Creon's plotting
His determination to uncover the truth whatever the cost
His trust in the gods' oracles, which he follows without question
questions.explanation: The drive that made Oedipus solve the Sphinx's riddle makes him keep questioning when others beg him to stop. His greatest strength is also what destroys him.

questions.stem: How does Jocasta's attitude to oracles change during the play?
options: She scorns them to comfort Oedipus, then later prays to Apollo for help
She trusts them at first, then loses faith once Oedipus is exposed
She mocks them throughout and refuses to pray to Apollo
She fears them at first, then laughs at them after Polybus is found alive
questions.explanation: Jocasta mocks prophecy in the second episode, yet she later brings offerings to Apollo's altar. Her shifting faith shows how fear works on her as the truth draws near.

questions.stem: What is ironic about Tiresias's physical blindness?
options: He is blind but can still read the omens in the birds of the sky
He is blind, yet he is the first to accuse Creon of plotting against the king
He is blind but pretends to see so that the king will trust him
He is blind but sees the truth, while sighted Oedipus cannot see it
questions.explanation: Oedipus mocks Tiresias's blindness, and Tiresias replies that Oedipus is the one who cannot see. By the end Oedipus too is blind, but knows the truth.

questions.stem: Who are the Chorus in Oedipus the King?
options: Servants of Jocasta, who report what happens inside the palace
Elders of Thebes, who comment on the action and react to it
Priests of Apollo, who travel from Delphi with the oracle's words
Soldiers of Corinth, who come to take Oedipus home to be king
questions.explanation: The Chorus speaks for the citizens of Thebes. Loyal to Oedipus, they move between hope and dread, and their odes reflect on pride, fate and the gods.

questions.stem: How does Oedipus treat those who try to stop his search?
options: He thanks them for their concern and asks the Chorus to decide what he should do
He hands the investigation to Creon so that he cannot be accused of bias
He becomes angry and suspicious, threatening Creon, Tiresias and the shepherd
He listens patiently to each of them and agrees to wait for a sign from the gods
questions.explanation: Oedipus accuses Tiresias and Creon of treason and has the shepherd threatened. His temper is part of what the Chorus seems to warn against when it sings of pride.

questions.stem: Where and how was Oedipus the King first performed?
options: At the Pythian Games in Delphi, in honour of Apollo
At a festival of Athena in Athens, as a hymn sung by priests
At a festival of Dionysus in Athens, as part of a drama competition
At the royal court of Thebes, as entertainment for a visiting king and his household
questions.explanation: Greek tragedies were staged at the City Dionysia, a religious festival, where playwrights competed. The play is usually dated to the 420s BC, and many scholars link its plague to the one that struck Athens in 430 BC.

questions.stem: Why did Sophocles' original audience already know how the story would end?
options: The story of Oedipus was a well-known myth that tragedies retold
The ending was announced by the Chorus before the play began
The play had been performed many times in Athens that same year
The audience were given a written summary when they arrived
questions.explanation: Greek tragedians reworked familiar myths. The suspense comes not from what happens but how, and the audience's knowledge creates constant dramatic irony.

questions.stem: How did Oedipus become King of Thebes?
options: He inherited the crown from his adoptive father
He solved the riddle of the Sphinx and freed the city
He married Jocasta after defeating Laius's army in battle
He was chosen by the oracle of Apollo at Delphi
questions.explanation: The Sphinx was killing Thebans until Oedipus answered her riddle. The grateful city made him king, and he married the widowed queen, Jocasta.

questions.stem: The philosopher Aristotle praised Oedipus the King because its reversal and recognition happen together. Which moment best shows this?
options: Jocasta's story of the three roads, which reveals his true parents
Creon's return from Delphi, which reveals to everyone at once that the killer is Oedipus
The Corinthian's news, meant to free Oedipus from fear, reveals who he really is
Tiresias's accusation, which Oedipus recognises as true at once
questions.explanation: Aristotle called these peripeteia (reversal of fortune) and anagnorisis (recognition). The messenger comes to bring good news and instead reveals the truth, turning Oedipus's fortune in a single scene.

questions.stem: How did Greek staging conventions shape the play?
options: Women played the female roles, and battles were staged in front of the audience
Actors wore everyday clothes, and deaths were shown in full view
Each part had its own actor, and the Chorus sang from offstage
Male actors in masks played all the parts, and violence happened offstage
questions.explanation: A small cast of masked male actors shared the speaking roles, with the Chorus singing and dancing. Deaths and injuries were reported, not shown, which is why a messenger describes Jocasta's death and Oedipus's blinding.

questions.stem: Which idea is most central to Oedipus the King?
options: Whether humans can escape the fate the gods have foretold
Whether a city should go to war to defend its honour
Whether wealth brings happiness to a king and his family
Whether a king should share power with his family
questions.explanation: Laius, Jocasta and Oedipus all try to escape prophecies, and their efforts bring them about. Yet Oedipus's own choices, such as pursuing the truth, are his.

questions.stem: Is Oedipus simply a puppet of fate? Which view is best supported by the play?
options: Oedipus has no real choice, because every action he takes is dictated by the oracle
Oedipus is free of fate, because the prophecy turns out to be false at the end
Oedipus is ruined by chance alone, since the gods play no part in what happens
The prophecy is fixed, but Oedipus freely chooses to pursue the truth and punish himself
questions.explanation: What Oedipus did years ago was foretold, but the investigation, his refusal to stop and his self-blinding are his own acts. Many readers find the tragedy in this mix of fate and choice.

questions.stem: How does the play use sight and blindness?
options: Blindness is shown as a gift the gods grant to the wisest and most faithful of kings
Sighted characters fail to see the truth, while the blind prophet sees it
Blindness stands for ignorance, so the blind prophet knows least
Sight stands for power, so Oedipus loses his throne with his eyes
questions.explanation: Tiresias is blind yet knows everything; Oedipus can see yet is ignorant. When he finally sees the truth, he blinds himself, completing the pattern.

questions.stem: Oedipus killed his father and married his mother without knowing who they were. How does the play treat his guilt?
options: He is declared innocent by the Chorus and is allowed to keep his throne and his family
He blames Apollo and insists that he bears no guilt himself
He is pardoned by Creon, who says his ignorance excuses him
He is polluted by the deeds and punishes himself, even though he acted unknowingly
questions.explanation: To the Greeks, killing a father and marrying a mother polluted a person and their city whatever their intentions. Oedipus accepts the pollution and the punishment, which gives him a terrible dignity.

questions.stem: What does the play suggest about human knowledge and power?
options: Even the cleverest and most powerful people cannot see their own lives clearly
Human intelligence can uncover the truth in time and so escape the plans of the gods
Power protects a king from suffering as long as he rules justly
Questioning the past is wrong, so Oedipus should have obeyed Jocasta
questions.explanation: Oedipus solved the Sphinx's riddle but cannot solve the riddle of himself. The play humbles human intelligence before forces it cannot control.

questions.stem: What is the main source of tension in the play?
options: Conflict: Oedipus and Creon fight a war over the throne
Romance: the love between Oedipus and Jocasta drives the plot
Dramatic irony: the audience knows the truth long before Oedipus does
Suspense: the audience waits to learn who killed Laius
questions.explanation: Oedipus's search is watched by people who know where it leads. Lines like his curse on the killer are charged with meaning he cannot see.

questions.stem: Why are Jocasta's death and Oedipus's self-blinding reported by a messenger rather than shown?
options: The Chorus is meant to witness them and report them to the audience
The messenger is used to slow the pace before the final scene
Greek tragedy kept violence offstage and let words make the horror vivid
The deaths happen at night, after the play's single day has ended
questions.explanation: The messenger's speech makes the audience imagine the scene inside the palace. Then the blinded Oedipus enters, so the result, not the act, is what we see.

questions.stem: What is the function of the choral odes between the episodes?
options: They reflect on the action and its meaning, voicing the city's hopes and fears
They advance the plot by revealing new facts that the characters do not know
They give the actors time to change masks, with little link to the plot
They speak for the gods, announcing what will happen in the next scene
questions.explanation: The Chorus prays to the gods, defends Oedipus, wonders about his birth and finally laments his fall. Their odes give the audience time to absorb what has happened.

questions.stem: The whole play takes place before the palace in Thebes, during a single day. What is the effect?
options: The audience is taken to Corinth and Delphi to see each event as it happened
The play feels static, since little of importance can happen in a day
Years of hidden history are uncovered in hours, which makes the fall swift and intense
The audience is shown many years of Oedipus's life, from his birth to his old age
questions.explanation: Everything Oedipus did happened long ago; the play shows only the day of discovery. Compressing time and place concentrates the tragedy into one terrible investigation.

questions.stem: In Fagles's translation, who warns Oedipus, 'This day will bring your birth and your destruction'?
options: Jocasta, as she begs him to stop
Creon, on returning from Delphi
The shepherd, before he confesses
Tiresias, during their angry quarrel
questions.explanation: Tiresias says this when Oedipus demands to know who his parents were. The same day will reveal who Oedipus's parents were and bring him down.

questions.stem: Oedipus declares, 'I count myself the son of Chance'. When does he say this, and what does it show?
options: After he is blinded; it shows he now accepts the prophecy as his fate
After Creon returns; it shows his fear that the plague will spread further
After Jocasta begs him to stop; it shows his pride on the edge of discovery
After the Sphinx is defeated; it shows his gratitude to the gods of Thebes
questions.explanation: Oedipus thinks Jocasta fears he is of humble birth. Calling himself a child of Chance shows his confidence just before he learns his fate was never chance at all.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest topic sentence for the prompt ''Oedipus is destroyed by his own character, not by the gods.' Discuss.'?
options: Sophocles suggests that Oedipus's fierce pursuit of truth, not the prophecy alone, brings about his fall
Oedipus the King is a Greek tragedy written by Sophocles and translated into English by Robert Fagles
This essay will discuss whether the gods or Oedipus are to blame in the famous play by the writer Sophocles
In Oedipus the King, Oedipus finds out that he killed his father, Laius, and married his mother
questions.explanation: A strong topic sentence takes a position on the prompt and points to what the paragraph will prove. The others state facts, announce or retell.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'Tiresias is blind and Oedipus is not.' How could this be turned into analysis?
options: List the other characters in the play who are not blind, such as Creon and Jocasta
Describe in order what happens in the scene after Tiresias leaves the stage
Explain how the contrast shows that true insight has nothing to do with physical sight
Add how old Tiresias is and how long he has served as a prophet to the kings of Thebes
questions.explanation: Analysis explains what a detail suggests. Linking the contrast to the theme of sight and blindness turns a fact into an argument.
